scenes.headline: How an agent rewrites its memories before using them
scenes.sub: MemHarness: check a retrieved memory against the current state, then act.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Minnow! Most agents paste a retrieved memory straight into context. MemHarness checks it against what's in front of it first. Here's how.

scenes.label: The idea
scenes.text: A retrieved memory is general; the current state is concrete. Compare the memory's source state with the live one, then keep, adapt or reject it.
scenes.say: The idea: memory is rebuilt, not replayed. Before acting, compare the state a memory came from with the state you're in, then keep it, adapt it, or reject it.

steps.say: Each memory pairs an abstract lesson with the observation it was learned from. The agent queries the bank and gets back the three closest.
Then the same seven billion parameter policy compares each memory's source state with the state it's in right now.
If it still fits, the memory passes through, or gets rewritten for the new state. If nothing fits, the policy says empty and falls back on its own reasoning.

steps.note: one policy plays all three roles
steps.say: Then it acts. One outcome reward, trained with GRPO, credits the rewrite and the action together.

scenes.title: ALFWorld success, by memory wiring
scenes.note: single paper, no seeds or variance reported
scenes.say: On ALFWorld, pasting raw memories into the trained policy scores seventy point one, below no memory at all. Reconstructing them scores eighty-five point two.

scenes.text: Memory helps only once it's checked against the present. Reconstruct, don't replay.
scenes.say: So a memory helps only once it's checked against the present. Reconstruct it; don't replay it.

recap: Each memory keeps the state it came from
One policy keeps, adapts or rejects it
Raw replay can do worse than no memory
scenes.say: To recap: keep the source state, let the policy judge the memory, and never just replay it.
